transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess what brings me in is… my body hasn’t felt like it’s really under my control. It’s been kind of scary, honestly. At first I was just moving constantly, like pacing around my apartment all night, back and forth, making these supper-club notes and plans, just writing things down and circling things and getting up again, like I couldn’t sit still even if I wanted to.

And now it’s almost the opposite. I feel so slowed down. Like even basic stuff takes me forever. My sister actually pointed out that it takes me ages just to get my shoes on, and I didn’t realize how bad it looked until she said it. It’s like my body either won’t stop moving or it barely moves at all, and I don’t feel like myself.
Have you been feeling unusually upbeat, irritable, or energized during any of these times when your body felt like it couldn’t slow down?

Yeah… yes. That was probably the strangest part, because it didn’t feel bad at first. After I got fired, I should’ve been devastated, or embarrassed, or scared about money, but instead I felt… almost lit up. Like this huge burst of energy came over me and I was weirdly excited, like, “Okay, this is actually perfect, now I can do all these bigger things.” I felt unstoppable, like I had this momentum and nobody else could see what I was seeing.

But it wasn’t just happy, exactly. It could turn really fast. If anyone questioned me or even gently suggested I slow down, I’d get furious. Like my sister would say, “Maybe think this through,” and I’d take it like she was trying to destroy my whole life. I’d snap at people, argue, raise my voice. It felt like they were standing in the way of something huge I was supposed to do. At the time it felt justified, but looking back, it was way more intense than the situation called for.

Have you experienced any distinct periods where your mood was unusually high, irritable, or you felt an intense surge of energy or drive to achieve specific goals, even if others didn’t understand them?

Yes. After I got fired, that’s when it really started. I didn’t react the way I think a normal person would. I felt… weirdly unstoppable, honestly. Like instead of being scared or ashamed, I was suddenly excited, like this was some kind of opening and I had all these plans I had to act on right away.

And it wasn’t just a vague good mood. It felt like this intense drive, like I knew exactly what I was supposed to do and everyone else was just too slow or too negative to understand it. If someone questioned me or told me to slow down, I’d blow up. I mean, really blow up, like they were personally trying to ruin my life or block me from doing something important.

At the time it felt completely justified, like I was defending myself and my future. But looking back, the reaction was way bigger than what people were actually saying. They’d just be concerned, and I’d take it as an attack.

During this time when you felt that intense drive and energy, did it last for at least four days straight, and was it so pronounced that people who know you well noticed something was off or it affected your ability to function normally?

Yeah, definitely longer than four days. I mean… it’s kind of embarrassing to say, because when I look back it wasn’t just a weekend or a few “weird” nights. This has been going on for about four months now, since right after I got fired from the restaurant.

At first I kept telling myself it was just stress, or that I was reacting to losing the job, but it didn’t pass after a few days. It just kept going, and it was obvious enough that people around me noticed I wasn’t acting like myself. My sister especially kept pointing it out, and I kept brushing her off because I thought she didn’t get it. But yeah… it lasted way past four days and it definitely affected how I was functioning normally.
During this time when you felt so energized and driven, did you find that you didn’t need as much sleep as usual, or that you were doing things that were unusually risky or out of character for you?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean, I know I felt like I had a lot of energy, and I was kind of constantly keyed up, but when you ask specifically about needing less sleep or doing risky things… I don’t know if I can point to that clearly.

Sleep is hard for me to judge because my schedule was already kind of messed up from working restaurant hours before, so I don’t know what “usual” even was for me anymore. Some nights I probably wasn’t sleeping great, but I don’t know if it was that thing where I truly didn’t need sleep, or if I was just wound up and stressed and telling myself I could keep going.

And with risky stuff… I guess I’d need to know what you mean by risky. I don’t want to overstate it and say yes if it’s not what you’re asking. I definitely wasn’t acting like myself in some ways, but I’m not sure I have a specific example that fits what you mean.

During that time when you felt so energized and driven, were you doing things that were out of character for you or that could be considered risky, like spending sprees, impulsive decisions, or taking on too many projects at once?

Yeah… when you put it that way, the biggest thing was the supper club idea. I don’t know if I’d call it “risky” exactly, but it was definitely out of character in how intense I got about it.

I started texting old coworkers constantly, like people I hadn’t talked to in a while, trying to get them on board. I was making spreadsheets for menus and costs and who could do what, planning tastings like they needed to happen immediately, reaching out to possible musicians, trying to recruit people all day and even late at night. It wasn’t like, “Oh, maybe this could be a fun idea someday.” It felt urgent, like if I didn’t move on it right then, I was wasting the chance of my life.

And I could tell people were kind of confused by how fast I was pushing it. I’d be sending long messages about what the concept should be, who we should invite, what the vibe would be, how we could make it bigger. I was acting like this whole thing had to come together right away, like everyone should just drop what they were doing and help me make it happen. Looking back, that’s not really how I usually approach things.
Was there a time when your mood was so high or irritable that it was clearly different from your usual self, and this lasted for at least a week?

Yeah. I mean, yes, there was. It was after I got fired, and it wasn’t just me being upset for a day or two. My mood was… weirdly high, almost excited, like I suddenly had this sense that I was going to do something huge and nobody else could see it yet.

I remember feeling unstoppable, like getting fired was somehow this sign that I was meant to move onto something bigger, which sounds kind of ridiculous when I say it now. But at the time it felt completely obvious to me. I wasn’t just “in a good mood,” though. It could flip really fast into me being angry. If anyone questioned what I was doing or told me to slow down, I’d take it like they were attacking me or trying to ruin my life.

Like, if my sister or someone said, “Maybe don’t rush into this,” I would blow up. Not just get annoyed — I’d feel this intense irritation, like they were standing in the way of this amazing thing I had to do. And that’s not really how I usually am. I can get defensive like anyone, but this was way more intense and it definitely lasted longer than a week.

After this period of high energy and intense drive, did you experience a time when your mood dropped significantly, and you felt persistently sad, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… definitely. It’s like after all that intensity, everything just kind of went dead or flat. I don’t even know if “sad” is the right word all the time, because sometimes it’s less like crying and more like I just can’t feel connected to anything.

The things that usually keep me steady don’t work right now. Cooking is a big one — normally I can get kind of lost in making something, thinking about flavors or plating or whatever, and it helps me feel like myself. But now I’ll look at ingredients or think about making something and it just feels like… nothing. Like I know I used to care, I know that was my thing, but I can’t make myself care about it.

Same with taking food photos, music, pickup soccer, even volunteering. Those were all things that usually made me feel grounded, or at least gave me some reason to get out of my own head. Now they just feel flat. I’ll try to put music on and it’s like background noise. I’ll think about going to play soccer and it feels pointless before I even get there. Volunteering used to make me feel useful, and now even that feels distant, like I’m going through the idea of it but not actually feeling anything from it.

It’s really unsettling, honestly, because it feels like I remember being a person who liked things, but I can’t access that feeling right now.
Did you experience a period of at least two weeks where you felt down or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, or lost interest in almost all activities?

The part I can say really clearly is the losing interest part. I don’t want to pretend I’ve tracked it perfectly day by day, but it’s been this ongoing thing where the stuff that usually keeps me steady just doesn’t land anymore.

Cooking is the biggest one, because that’s usually where I feel most like myself. Normally I can get into it — thinking about ingredients, taking food photos, putting music on while I cook — and now it’s like I’m looking at someone else’s hobbies. I know I used to care, I know it mattered to me, but I can’t make myself feel that.

And it’s not just cooking. Music feels like noise. Pickup soccer feels like too much effort and kind of pointless. Even volunteering, which usually makes me feel useful, feels flat. It’s like all the things that usually give me some structure or meaning are still there, but I can’t connect to them. So yeah, the loss of interest has been pretty strong.
